analysis.one_liner: Requires cars to detect and block drunk drivers and states to mandate ignition interlocks after convictions.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or a single cosponsor and died in House subcommittees when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Transportation, within 10 years, to set a vehicle safety standard so cars cannot be driven by someone over the legal alcohol limit. It also would have penalized states that refuse to require ignition interlock devices for at least 180 days on the vehicles of convicted drunk drivers, by holding back a growing share of their federal highway money.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the roads: drivers, passengers, cyclists, and pedestrians. The bill's own findings note alcohol-impaired driving killed 10,874 people in 2017 — about one-third of all highway deaths — and estimate that widespread alcohol-detection technology in cars could save roughly 59,000 lives and $343 billion over 15 years [S3]. States that adopted the interlock requirement would also see repeat drunk-driving offenses addressed by the 180-day device mandate [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Department of Transportation to issue, within 10 years, a federal motor vehicle safety standard that prevents a car from being operated when the driver's blood alcohol is above the legal limit, with requirements that the technology be accurate, fast, tamper-resistant, and work in extreme temperatures [S2][S3].

Pressures states to fight repeat drunk driving by withholding part of their federal highway aid — 1% in fiscal 2022, 3% in fiscal 2023, and 5% each year after — unless they require an ignition interlock device for at least 180 days on the vehicle of every person convicted of drunk driving; states that later comply get the withheld money back [S2][S3].

Targets the largest remaining cause of highway deaths: the bill's findings cite 10,874 alcohol-impaired driving deaths in 2017 and an estimated 59,000 lives and $343 billion in savings from widespread use of alcohol-detection technology in vehicles [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would have to install alcohol-detection technology meeting strict performance requirements in new vehicles, with costs likely passed into vehicle prices [S3]. State governments, which would lose a share of federal highway funds (up to 5%) if they decline to adopt the interlock mandate [S2]. And convicted drunk drivers, who would bear the cost of an ignition interlock on their vehicle for at least 180 days [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: New-car buyers, states, and convicted drivers

drawbacks.text: The vehicle mandate would add compliance costs for automakers — the bill requires technology that is reliable, accurate, unobtrusive, fast, tamper-proof, works in hot and cold extremes, and is easily maintained — and those costs would likely be passed on to new-car buyers [S3].

States that choose not to mandate ignition interlocks would see up to 5% of their federal-aid highway funds withheld, putting pressure on road projects and state budgets; the money is only returned if the state later complies, otherwise it lapses [S2][S3].

The federal standard depends on passive alcohol-detection technology that may not be proven within the 10-year deadline; a sensor that misreads a sober driver could strand them, which is why the bill itself demands the technology be accurate and fast before the standard takes effect [S3].
The interlock mandate creates a guaranteed market for interlock vendors, and the device rental costs fall on the convicted driver, adding to the penalties of a DUI conviction [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside is very large — a technology-based check on the leading cause of U.S. highway deaths, with the bill's own findings projecting about 59,000 lives saved over 15 years [S3]. The costs are real but comparatively modest: per-vehicle technology expenses passed to buyers, funding pressure on non-complying states, and device costs on offenders. The main honest concern is feasibility: the standard must be met by technology that does not yet exist at scale, so the rule's success would hinge on the sensor working flawlessly in real-world conditions. On balance the benefits clearly outweighed the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then to subcommittees, where nothing further happened before Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathleen Rice (D-NY) introduced the End Drunk Driving Act of 2019 on May 23, 2019 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day [S5].
The next day it was sent to the Highways and Transit Subcommittee and the Consumer Protection and Commerce Subcommittee — the last recorded action; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over the life of the Congress [S4], and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers avoided a federal mandate to engineer and install alcohol-detection technology in new cars, and state governments kept full control over their drunk-driving laws without risking highway funds. Road users gained nothing: the roughly 10,000 alcohol-impaired driving deaths the bill cited each year continued.

for.name: Rep. Kathleen Rice
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill in the House on May 23, 2019

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no further action after receiving the bill; it sat in their subcommittees until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the Democratic sponsor's bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have required every new car to carry alcohol-detection technology meeting strict accuracy and tamper-resistance standards within 10 years, a compliance cost likely passed to buyers. NHTSA was already partnering with automakers to develop the technology, which softened the burden [S3].

A federal requirement that states mandate interlocks for at least 180 days on every convicted drunk driver's vehicle would have created a large guaranteed market for device makers. The rental costs would fall on convicted drivers, not the public [S2][S3].

States refusing the interlock mandate would lose 1% to 5% of their federal-aid highway apportionments, pressuring road budgets. States that complied would keep full funding and get a new tool against repeat offenders [S2][S3].
